SEC15A-01.explanation: The relative pronoun "that" refers to "components," not to "one": the sentence says the balance spring belongs to the group of few components that are shaped by hand. The verb of the relative clause must therefore be plural. The passage is also set in the present ("Automated lathes now cut," "a technician may spend," "the watch keeps time"), so the verb must be present tense: "are still shaped." "is still shaped" is present but singular; it agrees with "one" (or with "The balance spring") rather than with the relative pronoun's antecedent "components." "was still being shaped" is singular and past. "were still being shaped" is plural but past (progressive), which conflicts with the present-tense description signaled by "now" and "may spend."

SEC15A-02.explanation: The digging went on "for many generations" and was already under way "by the time two young scholars arrived to excavate there in 1896." An action that continued up to a later past moment takes the past perfect (here progressive, because of the stated duration): "had been mining." "have been mining" is present perfect, which connects the action to the present, not to a moment in 1896; it cannot be paired with "by the time ... arrived." "were mining" is simple past progressive, which does not express an action continuing for a duration up to an earlier past point, so it cannot take "for many generations by the time ... arrived." "will have mined" is future perfect, which contradicts the past events described ("arrived ... in 1896," "were already gone").

SEC15A-03.explanation: The subject is "A single larch core"; the phrase "together with dozens of samples sawn from the beams of abandoned herders' huts" is an addition set off by commas and does not make the subject plural. The verb must be singular. It must also be active, because the core is doing the indicating and the verb takes the that-clause "that summers across the region turned abruptly colder" as its object: "strongly indicates." "strongly indicate" is active but plural; it agrees with "samples" or "huts," which sit inside the "together with" phrase. "is strongly indicated" is singular but passive; a passive verb cannot take the core as its subject and the that-clause as an object ("the core is indicated that ..." is ungrammatical). "are strongly indicated" is both plural and passive.

SEC15A-04.explanation: The sentence's subject is the whole infinitive phrase "To reconstruct the day-by-day weather of eighteenth-century Bohemia from the handwritten diaries of farmers, innkeepers, and village priests"; nothing else in the main clause can serve as its verb ("described" belongs to the "since" clause). The blank must supply a finite verb, and an infinitive-phrase subject is singular: "requires." "requiring" is a participle, so the sentence would have no main verb. "to require" is an infinitive and leaves the same fragment. "require" is finite but plural; it agrees with nearby plural nouns such as "diaries" or "priests," none of which is the subject.

SEC15A-05.explanation: The walls belong to "The vault's main tunnel," the subject of the sentence, which is singular; the plural noun "slopes" belongs to the mountain and is not what has walls. A singular possessive is needed: "its walls." "their walls" is possessive but plural; it would point to "slopes" (or "seeds"), which do not have walls in this sentence. "it's walls" uses the contraction of "it is," producing "surrounding it is walls," which is ungrammatical. "they're walls" is both plural and a contraction ("they are").

SEC15A-06.explanation: The subject "the rector" has two verbs, "recorded" and "copied," linked by the correlative pair "both ... and": the rector "both recorded ... and copied." Nothing should separate the parts of a compound predicate joined this way, so "churchyard and" is correct. "churchyard, and" puts a comma inside the "both ... and" construction, separating the second verb from its subject. "churchyard; and" uses a semicolon, which must join two independent clauses, but "and copied each entry ..." has no subject. "churchyard. And" starts a new sentence with "And copied each entry ...," which has no subject and is a fragment; it also leaves "both" without its partner.

SEC15A-07.explanation: "an island whose distance from the crowded capital reduced the danger of fire and ... also made it easier ..." is an appositive renaming "Murano." Its verbs "reduced" and "made" belong to the relative clause beginning "whose distance," so the phrase has no main verb of its own and cannot stand as a sentence. Because "Murano" is a proper name, the appositive is nonrestrictive and is set off with a comma: "Murano, an." "Murano an" omits the comma, running the name and the nonrestrictive appositive together. "Murano; an" uses a semicolon, which requires an independent clause on each side, but the appositive is not a clause. "Murano. An" makes "An island whose distance ... reduced ... and ... made ..." a separate sentence, which is a fragment because both of its verbs are inside the relative clause.

SEC15B-01.explanation: The subject is "The steel escapements," which is plural; the phrases "in the lone surviving prototype by a little-known Lancashire watchmaker and in the many later instruments built from copies of its drawings" only modify it, so the singular nouns "prototype" and "watchmaker" do not control the verb. The verb must therefore be plural. The phrase "since the first sea trials in 1774" describes an action that began in the past and continues into the present, which requires the present perfect. Only "have kept time" is both plural and present perfect. "has kept time" has the right aspect but is singular. "keep time" is plural but simple present, which cannot combine with "since the first sea trials." "keeps time" is both singular and simple present.

SEC15B-02.explanation: The subject is "the linen rags beaten into pulp in its stone vats." The rags did not do the collecting; the phrase "by itinerant peddlers" names who collected them, so the verb must be passive. The passage describes a mill that "operated ... in the 1340s" and peddlers who "sold" the rags, so the verb must also be past tense. "were collected" is passive and past. "are collected" is passive but present tense, which conflicts with the fourteenth-century frame. "have collected" is active, so it makes the rags the collectors and leaves "by itinerant peddlers" with no function, and its present perfect tense also clashes with the 1340s. "collected" leaves the sentence without a main verb: it reads as a second participle modifying "the linen rags," like "beaten," so the sentence becomes a fragment.

SEC15B-03.explanation: The subject is "the first such network in Europe," and the sentence dates the action precisely: "in the spring of 1857." An action completed at a specific past time takes the simple past, so "transmitted its" is correct. "has transmitted its" is present perfect, which links a past action to the present and cannot be paired with a specific completed past time such as "the spring of 1857." "transmits its" is present tense, and "will transmit its" is future tense; both place an event that the sentence dates to 1857 in the wrong time. The present-tense first sentence ("Modern forecasting depends") describes today, not the 1857 event.

SEC15B-04.explanation: The subject of the sentence is "The domesticated silkworm"; the material between the commas, "a moth bred for roughly five thousand years in China by generations of farmers tending mulberry groves," is an appositive, and "bred" and "tending" are participles, not main verbs. The sentence therefore still needs a finite main verb, and it must agree with the singular "silkworm" rather than with "farmers" or "groves." "depends entirely" is finite and singular. "depend entirely" is finite but plural, agreeing with the nearby plural nouns instead of the subject. "depending entirely" and "to depend entirely" are nonfinite forms, so with either one the clause before the colon has no main verb and is a fragment.

SEC15B-05.explanation: The first sentence is a statement: "Historians of cryptography have long puzzled over how ... envoy managed to read dispatches ..." The "how" clause is an indirect question embedded as the object of "puzzled over," so the sentence ends with a period, not a question mark. What follows, "The answer ... turns out to be simple bribery," is a separate independent clause. "possessed. The" correctly ends the statement and begins the new sentence. "possessed? The" punctuates the statement as though it were a direct question. "possessed, the" joins two independent clauses with only a comma, a comma splice. "possessed the" fuses the two clauses with no punctuation, and it misreads "the answer" as the object of "possessed."

SEC15B-06.explanation: The words after the blank, "its bronze, alloyed with far more tin than the founders had meant to add, proving too brittle to absorb the shock," contain no main verb: "had meant" belongs to the comparison inside the interrupting phrase, and "proving" is a participle. The group is therefore an absolute phrase explaining why the bell split, not an independent clause, and an absolute phrase at the end of a sentence is set off with a comma. "clapper, its bronze" does this. "clapper; its bronze" uses a semicolon, which must join two independent clauses, so the second part is a fragment. "clapper. Its bronze" makes that same phrase a sentence on its own, also a fragment. "clapper its bronze" runs the absolute phrase into "clapper" with no punctuation, so it reads as though "its bronze" continued the noun phrase "the clapper."

SEC15B-07.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is "Only the households drawing water from a single spring above the harbor," and its verb is "escaped." The phrase "drawing water from a single spring above the harbor" is restrictive: it identifies which households escaped, as "Only" signals, so it takes no punctuation, and nothing should separate the subject from "escaped." "households drawing" is correct. "households, drawing" inserts a single comma, which either treats the essential phrase as nonessential without the closing comma it would need or separates the subject from its verb. "households—drawing" has the same problem with a single dash. "households: drawing" uses a colon, which must follow a complete independent clause, but "Only the households" is not a clause; the colon also cuts the subject off from its verb.
